content.summary_of_the_paper: In order to increase the expressive power of GNNs, a lot of strategies used in many research have been seen, e.g., augmenting node/edge features by position/structural information. This paper focuses on the affinity metrics to achieve this purpose. Specifically the paper considers the statistics that arise from random walks in graphs, by exploring hitting/commute time between pairs of vertices, so that such a feature can be incorporated in the standard graph message passing neural network. It has been found that the richer vector-valued resistive embedding is quite effective in discriminating nodes etc.  In fact the distances between these embedding can reveal the hitting time etc, or in other words, the embedding method provides an alternative way to calculate the hitting/commute time according to the theoretical proof presented in the paper.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. By defining the resistive embedding, the paper claims that the resistive embedding can be used to calculate the hitting time (Lemma 4.3)
2. Thus instead of directly using hitting/commute time as node/edge features, the embedding has replace them in MPNN

Weakness:

1. The novelty is incremental. All the conclusion can trace back to Lovasz (1993), that is, the very important conclusion Res(u,v) = K_{uv}/2M and Res(u,v) = (1_u-1_v)L^*(1_u-1_v) where L^* is the pseudo-inverse of L.  As Res(u,v) = (1_u-1_v) L^{*/2}L^{*/2}(1_u-1_v), thus Definition 3.1 is straightforward. It is in fact r_v = L^{*/2}1_v or simply r_v = L^{-1/2}1_v.  Thus, all the conclusions in Section 4 are trivial.

2. Although the paper uses an example in Figure 1 to show that a MPNN using Res(u,v) can distinguish nodes in this particular graph, this does not prove it will be more expressive than MPNN without using these features. The reason is, we cannot simply say in all cases MPNN using Res(u,v) are always better than MPNN without using Res(u,v).  Unless I have missed something, I believe that the general claim (Theorem 3.7) cannot hold.

3. In the experiments, it is not clear how the new features are used in MPNN.  It is better to have detailed description. For example, (3)-7) in Section 5 do not clearly specify where the new features Res(u,v) and Embedding are used.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper has good readibility. In general the paper is well written. As pointed in the above Weakness 1, the originality of the work is limited.

Couple of minor comments for correction:

1. In Lemma 4.1, the last 1\leq j\leq m should be 1\leq i\leq m??

2. On page 16 of the Appendix, Lemma 4.3 and its proof are repeated and mixed up. Please clear it up.

3. It is not clear when a random projection in embedding is applied, how this is dealt in training (fixed or randomly applying each train step)?
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper does not provide sufficient novelty for ICLR. It can be regarded as re-interpretation of the early work from Lovasz (1993).
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper4400 by Reviewer siZ1

content.title: Response to Reviewer siZ1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for taking the time to provide us with insightful questions and comments. We respond to specific comments below:

1. The main contribution in Section 4 is to **obtain low-dimensional embeddings** that yield an efficient approximation of affinity measures, enabling their practical use in GNNs. This we show can be achieved via a clever _combination of the results of Lovász with dimensionality reduction techniques_. Furthermore, we posit a novel additive approximation result for hitting times (see Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4); Specifically, we show that the resistive embeddings can be used with Tetali’s formulation of hitting time to obtain an additive approximation to hitting time. As far as we know, Lemma 4.4 does not appear in the literature.

2.
You state that:

     > We cannot simply say in all cases MPNN using Res(u,v) are always better than MPNN without using Res(u,v).

     This is absolutely true, and this is not what we claim—we claim that the _expressive power of MPNN with Res(u, v) is strictly higher than that of MPNNs without_, in the following sense: First, since we _cannot decrease expressive power by adding features_, MPNNs with Res(u, v) are certainly at least as expressive as MPNNs without them. Secondly, since we demonstrate that there exist graphs that MPNNs with Res(u, v) can distinguish, but MPNNs without Res(u, v) cannot, it is implied that the overall expressive power of MPNNs gets increased by including Res(u, v). That is, for every possible pair of graphs to be distinguished, either adding Res(u, v) makes an MPNN able to distinguish them, or makes no difference. We are happy to discuss further on these points, or improve the clarity of the paper, if this would be helpful!

3. We have now added clarification on how the affinity-based measures are incorporated in the MPNNs (see Section 5 of the updated draft). In particular:
>We incorporate edge-based affinity features (e.g., effective resistances and hitting times) in $f_e$, while we incorporate node-based affinity features (e.g., resistive embeddings) in $f_n$. Note that node-based affinity features may also naturally be incorporated as edge features by concatenating the node features at the endpoints.

Regarding the minor comments:

1. Indeed, the line should read $1 \leq i \leq m$ and has been corrected in the new draft.

2. Thank you for noting the mix up in the appendix. The duplicate proof has been removed in the latest draft.

3. The random projections are applied only when the number of edges is sufficiently large; otherwise, it is faster to do an exact computation using a full matrix inversion. When random projections are used, they are applied at the beginning of training to compute a fixed set of resistive embeddings for each graph. However, note that the random rotation augmentation technique (discussed in Section 3.3) is applied separately at each training step.
Furthermore, we note that to provide further evidence of the efficacy of the random projections, we are now including the results of additional experiments, conducted on the ogbn-mag dataset, a large heterogeneous network consisting of **1,939,743 nodes** and **21,111,007 edges** (hence, even larger than ogbn-arxiv, with 11x as many nodes and 18x as many edges as ogbn-arxiv). Using our techniques on ogbn-mag _crucially requires the use of random projections_, due to the scale of the dataset.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a new MPNN variant that leverages affinity-based features. Specifically, they consider random walk-based statistics such as hitting time between nodes in order to augment edge features in the graph. To make this approach scalable to large datasets, the paper proposes to employ random projections using Gaussian matrices for these affinity-based features to remain of manageable dimensionality. The paper claims that expressivity beyond WL-1 can be achieved, which is a nice property, however there are existing GNN variants that achieve this as well, so the novelty of this property for a new GNN variant is limited.
In the experiments, improvements over the vanilla MPNN can be seen, while the method seems to perform reasonable across several datasets, in particular showing new SOTA results on the OGBG-PCQM4Mv1 benchmark which I think is interesting. At the same time, the OGB benchmark page states that v1 is outdated, and that v2 should be used. So it would be interesting to see, if the proposed method also performs competitive on the current v2 (where probably most new methods are tested on), compared to the older v1 version.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Good contribution to scale random walk-based features to large-scale GNNs
- Paper is clearly written.
- Mixed-Ok experiments, but new SOTA on a large-scale benchmark (although it's an outdated version)

Weaknesses:
- Slightly out of touch with literature, amongst others e.g. Topological Graph Neural Networks have previously shown expressivity beyond 1-WL, plausibly could also solve the same example graph (Fig 1). This paper used a mini experiment on synthetic graphs to demonstrate that it can distinguish graphs that previous methods couldn't. This would be an easy way to credibly demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method against existing methods that improve expressivity. If this is not the case, then the claims about improving expressivty need to be toned down, e.g. it could be a nice property, but is it not a novel contribution to the GNN literature.
- previous Random walk based methods are not discussed. At least refer to Random walk kernels, and ideally compare to previous GNN variant that leverage random walks, e.g. Random Walk Graph Neural Networks (Neurips 2020).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written. One thing that would drastically increase the exposition and understanding "at a glance" of the method would be a clear overview figure.

To my knowledge, the proposed method has some novelty.

Due to late submission, I did not have time to check code for reproducibility.


Minor details: 
3.3. "where W are the non-negative edge weights" --> state dimensionality of W
L4.1 --> this looks weird. E.g. o(1) I suppose should be O(1)? I would reformulate in the standard way using bounds instead of equal signs (i'm not even sure if that is correct this way).
5.3 why are there almost no baslines in OGBG-MOLPCBA? I would expect to see at least GIN, GAT, GCN.
5.4 The number of layers is imho quite useless. If possible, it would be more informative to show runtime (at training or inference), memory costs, flops, CO2, #parameters, basically anything but #layers.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, the paper makes an interesting point that random-walk based features can be used to augment GNNs to improve performance. Random walks have been around in Graph ML for decades, e.g. with random walk kernels, which suffered from excessive runtimes. Therefore, the fact that random-walked based features show beneficial results on a large-scale benchmark is indeed promising.
However, there are several issues with the current submission, that I believe the authors need to address before publication is warranted:

- Either show (e.g. with synthetic experiment on graphs that are hard to distinguish) that the proposed method performs better than previous methods that increase expressivity (e.g. topology-aware GNN variants) to then more strongly claim that this method (of increased expressivity) is superior to existing works. Else, tone down the expressivity content, as simply going beyond 1-WL on its own is not a major novel finding at this time, albeit a nice side-property to mention.

- Several related pieces of literature are not mentioned nor compared to: in terms of expressiveness, TopoGNN (ICLR 2022), re random walks: random walk kernels, and random walk GNNs (Neurips 2020). It would be interesting to see how random walk GNNs perform as a baseline. Also, GIN would be a stronger baseline than simply GCN.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 46iR
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments and questions. We address specific comments below.

1. There are a few considerations that may guide the choice of which affinity measures to use. For very large graphs with a high number of nodes/edges, memory constraints may require sticking to scalar features (e.g., effective resistance, hitting time), as one may not be able to store multidimensional vector embeddings for every node. In cases where memory is not a bottleneck, one may be guided by whether one expects the given task to make more use of local structure or global structure — if the task involves the latter, it would make a stronger case for using resistive embeddings that may offer some “positional” context of each node within the graph. In comparison, using solely the scalar measurements would not offer a lot of flexibility for globally incorporating information across the graph (beyond the affinity metric itself). In the case of the PNA dataset, we note that training is over a variety of tasks, which exploit both local and global properties; hence, one can expect to benefit from using both the scalar and vector features, and we indeed observe this in the results.

2. Thank you for the suggestion. In the updated draft, we have now added further explanation to the tables displaying comparisons to SPD baselines (see Table 7). We would be happy to incorporate any other suggestions you may have for improving the exposition and clarity of this section.

3. We have now updated the PDF with the **GSN baseline** (from Bouritsas et al) for ogbg-molhiv (ROC-AUC of 77.99 ± 1.00). Furthermore, as mentioned in the summary response, we have conducted an additional set of experiments in which we **combine substructure/subgraph counts with affinity measures**. In particular, inspired by the approach of Bouritsas et al, we use k-cycles (for k = 3, 4) and k-paths (k = 3) as motifs and incorporate the resulting counts as features in an MPNN. We compare the results of using (a.) just these subgraph features, and (b.) using the subgraph features in conjunction with affinity measures. The results are below (ROC-AUC, higher is better), suggesting that affinity measures do, indeed, provide a performance lift to the ROC-AUC beyond just substructure counts:
	
	- _MPNN + substructure features_: 76.41 ± 0.42
	- _MPNN + substructure features + affinity measures_: **78.50 ± 0.51**

4. _Preprocessing times_: We note that the preprocessing times are quite short for the molecular datasets, as the number of nodes in such graphs is low — in particular, for ogbg-molpcba, preprocessing takes 15 minutes, while for the large-scale PCQM4Mv1, it takes < 1 hr. Perhaps more interesting is ogbn-arxiv, due to its much larger graph size (**169k nodes and 1.2M edges**) — here, **preprocessing takes less than an hour** with a MacBook Pro 2019 on 8-cores using Combinatorial MultiGrid linear system solver.

5. Effective resistances enjoy stronger robustness properties than other measures. For example, features based on shortest path distance or subgraph counting can change drastically even with an addition (or removal) of a single edge. On the other hand, for a connected graph, we can prove that adding a new, single edge can only change the effective resistance between any pair of nodes (not only edges) by a factor of at most 3/2, whereas the removal of an existing edge e can change the effective resistances between any pair by at most a factor of 1/(1-Re). For example, in the ogbn-arxiv graph, more than 95% of the edges have Re < 0.5, which means the removal of any such edge will increase the effective resistances by at most a factor of 2.

content.title: Thank You and Summary of Updates
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for taking the time to provide us with valuable feedback on our submission. While we respond to each reviewer individually, we first note the following high-level summary of major changes:

1. We have now conducted **additional experiments** that include results on the _ogbn-mag_ dataset, a large heterogeneous network consisting of **1,939,743 nodes** and **21,111,007 edges**. Note that this is an even larger dataset than the already-included ogbn-arxiv (with **11x as many nodes** and **18x as many edges**). We follow the model setup of the official OGB reference implementation (see graph_saint.py here), which uses mini-batch R-GCN training using the GraphSAINT algorithm. For comparison, we have tested the same model but with resistive embeddings and effective resistances included as node and edge features, respectively, thus allowing us to make greater use of the JL-based computational speedup trick mentioned in the paper. The results show that affinity measures offer a significant improvement and are as follows (test accuracy, higher is better):

   - _Baseline_: 47.51% ± 0.22
   - _With affinity measures_: **47.99% ± 0.23**

2. We have additionally added **GNN baselines** that incorporate _substructures, topological information, random walks_, etc., including models like GSN, HIMP, GRWNN. On ogbg-molhiv, the results are as follows (ROC-AUC, higher is better):

	- _GSN_: 77.99 ± 1.00
	- _HIMP_: 78.80 ± 0.82
	- _GRWNN_: 78.38 ± 0.99
	- _Affinity measures (ours)_: **79.13 ± 0.358**

3. Furthermore, for ogbg-molpcba, we provide the following comparisons (Mean Average Precision, higher is better):

	- _GCN_: 24.24 ± 0.34
	- _GIN_: 27.03 ± 0.23
	- _DeeperGCN_: 27.81 ± 0.38
	- _HIMP_: 27.39 ± 0.17
	- _Affinity measures (ours)_: **28.32 ± 0.13**

4. In order to better understand the interplay of affinity measures with substructure/subgraph features, we have also shared the results of **additional experiments** that incorporate substructure counts as features (both in combination with and without affinity measures). In particular, inspired by the approach of Bouritsas et al, we use k-cycles (for k = 3, 4) and k-paths (k = 3) as motifs and incorporate the resulting counts as features in an MPNN. We compare the results of using (a.) just these subgraph features, and (b.) using the subgraph features in conjunction with affinity measures. The results for the ogbn-molhiv dataset are below (ROC-AUC, higher is better), suggesting that affinity measures do, indeed, provide a performance lift to the ROC-AUC beyond just substructure counts:
	
	- _MPNN + substructure features_: 76.41 ± 0.42
	- _MPNN + substructure features + affinity measures_: **78.50 ± 0.51**


Additionally, we have uploaded a revised PDF incorporating various changes in response to the reviewers.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
__Summary.__ This paper seeks to extend the expressive power of GNNs beyond the 1-WL graph isomorphism test by adding distance and connectivity information. More specifically, the authors propose to use resistance embeddings to enrich the node features, as well as effective resistance and hitting times to enrich the edge information used by the GNN. Resistance embeddings are then considered as additional features and appended to the original node features before being fed into a GNN. To reduce the dimensionality of these embeddings, the authors propose using random projections (straightforward application of the Johnson Lindenstrauss lemma). 

 __Overall comments.__ The reviews on this paper are lukewarm at best. While the experiments presented show a marginal improvement of the performance of standard GNN methods when adding these additional features, the method hasn’t been deemed extremely novel by the reviewers. To some extent, this approach is quite straightforward: after the plethora of methods that try to use additional information to guide further the GNN (eg. Shortest path distance, subgraph counts), effective resistances come as natural new candidates. This sparked an interesting conversation during the rebuttal, in which reviewers urged the authors to compare their methods further against other techniques of the same type (eg adding subgraph features of the same type, shortest path distances, etc), which the authors have done during the rebuttal. Overall, this seems to highlight that a better way of framing the paper would be to show that effective resistance, hitting times, etc, provide a richer set of features (potentially more tractable) than subgraph counts, or perhaps less robust to noise (which they could check with synthetic experiments for instance)--- rather than suggesting a new technique whilst offering too little perspective as to its comparative advantage with existing approaches. __Consequently, we advise the authors to re-format their paper, and will advise a rejection of the paper for now. __
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: The method is not novel enough. To be published, it would require the authors to make a little bit more of a case for the method --- in particular, showing its robustness to noise for instance, or clearly expliciting what the advantage over other techniques (subgraph counts, shortest path distance) would be. The authors have already made substantial headway in this direction through the rebuttal, but the paper needs to be perhaps reformatted to highlight these aspects.
content.summary_of_AC-reviewer_meeting: The reviewers agreed on the "straightforwardness" of the method and the lack of novelty of the approach: the latter seems to be more of an "engineering" approach rather than a novel method. The reviewers recommended the use of synthetic experiments to make a more salient case for the method.
